metadata.title: Material resources, school climate, and achievement variations in the Philippines_ Insights from PISA 2018

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the OECD public-use PISA 2018 dataset restricted to 15-year-old students in the Philippines (7233 students in the full reading/math models; 6040–6386 in models with student-level attendance). The manuscript does not report applying PISA sampling weights or any replicate-weight variance estimation, nor does it name any weight variables from the PISA database. Because the analysis is conducted with hierarchical linear models (students nested in schools) rather than ML algorithms, the paper’s omission of explicit weighting details limits interpretability for population-representative inference. Analysts using the PISA microdata should apply the appropriate student sampling weights (and replicate weights if variance estimation is required) when estimating uncertainty, and should ensure the nested structure (students within schools) is respected in the estimation framework.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper describes PISA plausible values (ten PVs) and states that it reports results from the first plausible value for simplicity, implying a single-PV analysis. However, it does not document how missing questionnaire or index components (e.g., composite indices derived from principal component analysis) were handled, nor whether cases were excluded listwise or imputed. Given PISA’s typical item nonresponse, this is a reporting gap that affects reproducibility and could bias estimates if missingness is systematic.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the OECD public-use PISA 2018 dataset and restricted it to 15-year-old high school students in the Philippines. The analytic sample includes 7233 students from 187 public and private schools, combining student-level questionnaire data with school-principal questionnaire data. The dependent variables are standardized PISA reading and math test scores, and the study reports models with reduced N when student-level attendance is included (Number of students: 6386 for reading Model 5; 6040 for reading Model 6; 6386 for math Model 5; 6040 for math Model 6). No additional explicit exclusion rules for missing data are described.

main_findings.target_variable: Reading achievement (standardized test score; single plausible value)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Hierarchical linear models (HLM). Model 1: Level 2 variance share <40% (overall variance: Level 1 4090.88 vs Level 2 2183.69). Model 2 (materials): Level 2 % variance explained 19.30; materials coefficient −20.42 (SE 3.39), p<0.001. Model 3 (attendance/discipline): attendance coefficient −19.03 (SE 4.46), p<0.001; discipline coefficient 11.23 (SE 4.52), p<0.05. Model 6 (full): Level 2 % variance explained 52.90; Level 1 % variance explained 10.00; significant predictors include materials, school attendance, student attendance (all negative) and private school, female, SES (all positive), all p<0.001 where stated.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Philippines (15-year-olds) reading the study leveraged material resource constraints, attendance climate deficit, student attendance problem, school type, and socioeconomic status to predict reading achievement, finding that material and attendance-related constraints were significantly negatively associated with reading scores while private schooling, being female, and higher SES were significantly positively associated. This indicates that prioritizing material support and attendance-focused school climate interventions may narrow achievement gaps linked to socioeconomic disadvantage, though the study reports associations rather than causal effects.

main_findings.target_variable: Math achievement (standardized test score; single plausible value)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Hierarchical linear models (HLM). Model 1: >70% of overall variance at student level (Level 1 variance 4266.70 vs Level 2 variance 1902.70). Model 2 (materials): materials coefficient −17.07 (SE 3.25), p<0.001. Model 3 (attendance/discipline): attendance coefficient −17.98 (SE 4.19), p<0.001; discipline coefficient 10.73 (SE 4.24), p<0.05. Model 5 (adds student attendance): student attendance coefficient −17.66 (SE 0.82), p<0.001; Model 6 (full): Level 2 % variance explained 46.75 and Level 1 % variance explained 11.67. In Model 6, school attendance problem and student attendance problem were negative, while private school, female, and SES index were positive and significant at p<0.001.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Philippines (15-year-olds) math the study leveraged material resource constraints, attendance climate deficit, student attendance problem, school type, and socioeconomic status to predict math achievement, finding that attendance-related problems and material constraints were significantly negatively associated with math scores while private schooling, being female, and higher SES were significantly positively associated. This indicates that improving attendance and strengthening material learning conditions—especially in disadvantaged schools—may reduce within-school and between-school math disparities, though causality cannot be inferred from the correlational HLM design.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2018 microdata for the Philippines, restricting to 7233 15-year-old students nested within 187 public and private schools, and uses standardized reading and math test scores as outcomes. It constructs school-level indices for material resource constraints and school climate deficits (attendance and discipline) and includes student-level attendance, gender (female), and an OECD SES index. The authors fit hierarchical linear models and report that most variance is at the student level (reading: Level 1 variance 4090.88 vs Level 2 2183.69; math: Level 1 4266.70 vs Level 2 1902.70). For reading, material constraints and attendance problems are significantly negative (e.g., materials coefficient −20.42, p<0.001; attendance climate −19.03, p<0.001), while private school, female, and SES are positive (p<0.001). For math, attendance problems and material constraints are also negative (e.g., attendance climate −17.98, p<0.001; student attendance −17.66, p<0.001), with private school, female, and SES positive (p<0.001). Limitations include reporting only the first plausible value and not documenting missing-data handling or survey-weight application, so results should be interpreted as associations rather than causal effects.
